rationale: B wins because it finds one more genuinely useful altitude: "One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" is a sharper trade story than A's cleaner but more expected margin/profit/labor trio. A's best line, "A still-unprofitable public chain is betting the path to profit runs through automation," is strong, but B pairs that same markets angle with the rollout-format story, "not a pilot," and a concrete later data play. The caveat: B flirts with unsupported category context; A is tighter on the facts.
gaps_in_A: "Sweetgreen says its robot-assembled stores run higher margins than human-run ones" is accurate but a little too close to the company disclosure; it needs a sharper outside tension beyond 'the comparison itself.'
The first two angles overlap: "higher margins than human-run ones" and "path to profit runs through automation" both ride the same margin claim, just with different desks.
"If a labor-automation or restaurant-earnings story is live right now" is useful, but it punts instead of naming the missing peg as a blocker for anything beyond trades/markets.
A misses the rollout-format angle: putting Infinite Kitchen in "most new stores" is not just economics, it is a store-model shift.
gaps_in_B: "automation live mostly in pilots and demo units" is plausible industry context, but it is not in the supplied update. Don't smuggle beat lore in as fact.
"the beat rarely gets" is an unsupported flourish. It makes the category angle sound bigger than the evidence proves.
"One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" is strong, but B admits "This angle does not exist until that data does"; that makes it a future reporting package, not an immediate pitch.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the markets angle. This is profitability/unit economics, not financing mechanics.
